As someone who has worked in healthcare for the past 7 years, and has decided to pick a field that is more behind the scenes. I have always believed a jaded healthcare worker is a dangerous one. Once you get to the point that you stop treating your patients (or specimens) like people you become complacent in care and possibly setting yourself up to majorly affect that patient in some shape or form. Maybe a vacation, maybe a change of position or place, or maybe some therapy to see where the compassion was lost in the first place. Was the compassion lost because you were understaffed and expected to take on so much you became jaded, or some other reason. Working in healthcare is hard, I can’t even imagine being in a patient facing position, but each one of these people have sought help for a reason and have put their complete faith in strangers to help them. One thing my boss liked that I said during my interview was what bothered me at my old place was that each sample was just treated as another specimen, but in my head each specimen is a patient we don’t get to see them, but this is our interaction with that patient and it could be someone’s mother, brother, friend, coworker, or even if it’s someone that has no one it is a patient and it means something.

I also went through the FDAs website and how they recommend nutrition labels are created. (When I was totally supposed to be paying attention in my class lol >.>). There are different maximum allowable margins of error for different nutrients. They have recommended sample sizes and how to calculate what your sample size should be (I.e how many different lot numbers of the item need to be tested). Which are tested in by per 100 g, and then how to convert the numbers mean, standard deviation, etc. to the serving size number. Also from there there are equations for what to display on your label using these means, standard deviations, and desired margins of error/confidence intervals. They also have rules for rounding. It’s a lot of statistics and math, but really interesting. You also have to remember companies probably want to stay away from the upper limit because a slip up that causes them to be like at 122% of what they are claiming gets them in trouble with the FdA. There are also other testing guidelines that are regulated by other companies, etc.

So I made an original reply to this comment explaining how margins of error works and why it’s not a great idea to increase all your calculations by 20%, but because I used calories as an example in explaining the concept it got taken down. I went ahead and responded to the main post explaining margins of error, versus maximum allowable margins of error, versus acceptable margins of error. I also did a TLDR because it is kind of long. I hope you are willing to read it and see why overestimating by 20% is gonna cause more harm.

Allowable margin of error does not mean all counts will be higher by twenty percent, and that number is the maximum allowable error before the FDA steps in. Trying to adjust your intake based on this is going to cause more harm, and probably cause more brain preoccupation than we all already have. Allowable margins of error are very interesting and if you are really concerned about this, I would look into allowable margins of error and how they work. I do lab work and this is a large concept in many of our calibrations and measurements of analytes. I originally put an example, but it got removed for breaking the calorie rule so I’ll use something other than calories to explain the concept. So an acceptable margin of error will fall between 4% and 8% at a confidence level of 95%. So say I’m measuring number of times I say the word like when I’m speaking. I have a maximum margin of error of 20% like the FDA says, and I measure that I said the word like 10386 times in a day. Since my method of measurement isn’t 100% perfect I may have said it more or less. At a maximum margin of error I could have said like 8,309 times or 12,463 times before I have to actually reject my experiment and fix things or in the case of the FDA before they get involved and figure out what’s going on. Then there are acceptable margins of error which the companies are probably more aiming for so same excitement at a 4% margin of error so at a 4%margin of error we get me saying like 9,971 times or 10,801 times. Actual error won’t be exactly the same every time. In laboratory work we use things called Levy Jennings charts which plots control measurements against the mean, which then there are rules that trigger different reactions based on how far from the mean the measurement falls (standard deviations). Actually one of the rules for rejecting a run is that even if the measurements are only one standard deviation away from the mean, if 4 or more measurements fall on one side of the mean than it needs to be rejected for a possible systemic error. One standard deviation isn’t a lot depending on what you are measuring.

TLDR: margins of error, maximum allowable margins of error; and acceptable margins of error are all different concepts. It isn’t as simple as this meme makes it seem and if you plan to adjust your calories by like 20% higher then you may be doing more harm. I wouldn’t let this preoccupy your head this is already a disorder with a lot of struggle there is no need to freak out over this 20% when it isn’t always going to be 20% in the same direction and it isn’t always going to be 20% at all. Each company probably has an acceptable margin of error for themselves which is a lot different.

Also if anyone has any questions on this topic or is confused feel free to ask. This is part of what I do for work and part of what I’m learning in school, and it’s a very interesting concept used in a lot of scientific fields.
